name: 5W 0.33 ohm wirewound resistor
notes:
Decode: 5W = 5 watt, R33 = 0.33 ohm, J = +/-5%. Twenty in stock.

Useful for: current sensing (0.33 ohm x 15 A = 4.95 V - good range for shunt sensing), emitter degeneration, ballast, dummy load, LED current limiting at high current.

CAUTION: at 5 W into 0.33 ohm, I(rms) = sqrt(P/R) = 3.9 A continuous. Above that it cooks. Short pulses allow much more.

notes:
Beken BK3231Q is a low-power 2.4 GHz SoC (commonly Bluetooth or proprietary RF - confirm which). Mounted on a half-mini PCIe-shaped card with gold edge contacts, so it is almost certainly a pre-built module pulled from a laptop or device rather than a bare chip.

UNVERIFIED: whether BK3231Q is Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, or a proprietary 2.4 GHz protocol. Beken part numbers are not self-describing and I have not read the datasheet. Do not assume BT.

The 16.06 MHz crystal is unusual - standard BT crystals are 16.0 or 26.0 MHz. 16.06 suggests a specific PLL requirement.

name: TI TFP410 DVI/HDMI transmitter (on carrier PCB)
pkg: TQFP-64 (PAP suffix) on a small carrier PCB with mounting holes and pin headers
notes:
TI TFP410 = PanelBus DVI transmitter. Takes parallel digital video in (24-bit RGB + syncs) and outputs TMDS (DVI/HDMI electrical). 165 MHz pixel clock, up to 1600x1200 / 1080p.

This part was extremely common on laptops and media boxes - it converts the internal digital video bus into a DVI signal. The carrier PCB it is mounted on is likely a breakout from one of those.

IMPORTANT: TFP410 outputs DVI-P (TMDS), NOT HDMI. It does not carry audio and has no HDCP. For a modern display you need a DVI-to-HDMI adapter cable - passive, electrically compatible.

Useful for: driving a monitor from a custom FPGA/MCU digital video source, retro computer video output, or as a test signal generator if fed a known pattern.
qs: What is the carrier board's pinout - does it break out the parallel input?
Is there an I2C control header (TFP410 needs I2C to configure if not strapped)?
1896 module or a bare chip on a generic breakout?

name: Lattice ispLSI 2032 CPLD
notes:
Lattice ispLSI 2032: 32 macrocells, 2000 PLD gates, 5 V, in-system programmable. The '80' in 80LJ = 80 MHz. LJ = PLCC package.

This is the missing piece for the ISA bridge: a CPLD that can replace the whole glue-logic+state-machine design. 5 V tolerant, fast enough for an 8 MHz ISA bus, and reprogrammable so the bus timing can be tuned without rewiring.

CAUTION: ispLSI is the OLD Lattice family (pre-MachXO). Programming needs the right cable (ispDOWNLOAD or a compatible JTAG arrangement) and the old ispLEVER software, which is Windows-only and long unsupported. Verify a programming path exists BEFORE designing around it.

Physical signs of wear: diagonal scratch, residue along one edge. May have been desoldered - test for bent pins before use.
qs: Is there an ispDOWNLOAD cable or compatible programmer in stock?
Does an ispLEVER install exist anywhere that still runs?
Test socket the PLCC-44 to confirm it is alive

name: HP HCTL-1100 motion control IC
notes:
Hewlett-Packard HCTL-1100: a complete general-purpose motion controller on a chip. Contains a position feedback processor, a programmable digital filter/compensator, a profile generator (trapezoidal velocity), and PWM or 8-bit DAC command outputs to a motor drive. Interfaces to an encoder via quadrature inputs; talks to a host in parallel or serial.

Significance: it is a standalone single-axis motion controller that does not need a PC at all - you can feed it targets and let it close the loop. That is a much easier first motion project than reverse-engineering an ISA card.

IMPORTANT: this is 1990s HP silicon, long discontinued. Datasheet is public (HP application notes AN-1000 series) but must be read before wiring.

Needs: quadrature encoder, motor drive, 5 V supply, and a host interface chosen (parallel or serial).
qs: Do we have more than one? Multi-axis needs one HCTL-1100 per axis.
Encoder: do we have a quadrature encoder from the salvage pile to pair with it?
Read HP AN-1000-series app notes before designing

notes:
Called 'nRF24' by Mark - that is the trade name these are sold and known under, so the name stands.

TECHNICAL CLARIFICATION (not a correction of the name): the pictured boards carry a 13.56 MHz crystal and an etched meander antenna, which is the HF RFID / NFC band (ISO14443 Mifare, ISO15693, NFC) - not the 2.4 GHz band of a true nRF24L01 chip. So the family name and the radio band do not match on the pictured units; the name is a form-factor convention.

Function depends on the IC marking, not visible in these photos. Common parts in this shape: MFRC522 (SPI), PN532 (I2C/SPI/UART, full NFC), RC522 clones.

name: TI TMS320F28069F Piccolo microcontroller
markings: TMX320F28069FNA (TMX = TI pre-production/lot prefix; read from second enlarged photo)
notes:
Texas Instruments TMS320F28069F - C2000 Piccolo series real-time microcontroller.

Key specs (verify against datasheet before design): C28x core at up to 90 MHz, 256 KB flash, 100 KB RAM, on-chip 12-bit ADC, enhanced PWM (ePWM) and capture (eCAP) modules, CAN, SPI, I2C, UART, InstaSPIN-FOC support (the F suffix denotes InstaSPIN).

WHY THIS MATTERS: this is a modern, fast, programmable MCU with dedicated motor-control peripherals and a proper ADC. It is a far better motion-control platform than reverse-engineering 1990s ISA cards - it can close a servo loop, read an encoder, and generate ePWM directly. qty 2.

Programmable via TI CCS + XDS110 (or compatible) debugger. Needs 3.3 V, a 20 MHz crystal, and the BOOT pins configured.

Note: the earlier reading (10X / 30F28009F / 02A700 / 64) was OCR noise on a worn etch of this same part - 320F28069F was being misread. Both photos are the SAME chip, not two.

PROVENANCE: free TI sample, never used (Mark, 2026-11-14).

BLOCKER: no XDS110 debugger in stock. Options: (a) buy a clone XDS110 (~cheap, works with CCS), (b) check whether an XDS100v2-class or any C2000-compatible JTAG adapter is in the stash, (c) the chip has a boot-from-serial path - possible but painful.

Do not plan work around this until a programming path is confirmed.
qs: Programming path: XDS110 clone, or a C2000-compatible adapter in stock?
20 MHz crystal and 3.3 V regulator available?
Which of the two chips goes to the motor bench?

name: Lantronix XPort Direct+ (ethernet-serial bridge)
markings: PN XPD1001000-01 / Rev B11 / MAC 00-20-4A-A8-54-A0 / Made in Thailand / Date 08W42
pkg: Embedded module, RJ45 on one end, USB-style body, 3.3 V header power
notes:
Ethernet-to-serial bridge module. RJ45 on one side, TTL UART on the other: a device's serial port becomes a TCP socket.

Note the 'Direct+' variant is an embedded module (RJ45-ended USB stick form), not a general-purpose USB adapter - its I/O is TTL serial, powered from a header at 3.3 V.

Config typically via Lantronix DeviceInstaller (Windows), or over serial with escape sequences.

MAC printed on the label: 00-20-4A-A8-54-A0. The documented default telnet password scheme is a suffix of the MAC - verify against the manual for this firmware revision before relying on it.

Use: network-enable a UART device (Propeller, UBW32, motion controller) without adding an ESP32. qty 1.
qs: How many? (one shown)
Confirm default password scheme from Lantronix manual for Rev B11
